paper_title: SimVTA: Simulation-Grounded Video-Trajectory Alignment for Driving World Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Driving world action models (WAMs) learn from paired trajectories and future observations. Post-training with reinforcement learning allows the policy to explore alternative trajectories and improve planning using driving rewards. However, driving logs contain future videos only for the recorded trajectories, leaving these alternatives without corresponding visual supervision. Thus, we introduce SimVTA, a simulation-grounded post-training framework that combines trajectory optimization with video supervision. First, we sample candidate trajectories for each observation and use a real-world simulator (e.g., World Engine) to render future videos for high-reward candidates in real-world scenes reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). This provides trajectory-matched supervision independent of the model's own predictions. Under a limited rendering budget, we prioritize video supervision for higher-error futures among these rendered candidates. Finally, we optimize trajectory planning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and use a flow-matching loss on the matched videos to update shared representations. At inference time, the model predicts trajectories directly, without simulator calls. On NAVSIM v1, applying SimVTA to a WAM initialization improves PDMS from 86.2 to 91.3 (+5.1). It achieves 88.2 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and an average HD-Score of 38.8 in closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM. Ablations show that updating shared representations with video supervision improves planning, while prioritizing higher-error futures among high-reward trajectories further improves performance.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Driving WAMs combine future-scene prediction with trajectory planning for the ego vehicle. Predicting future frames provides dense visual supervision that complements sparse trajectory targets and helps models learn representations for planning (Li et al., 2025b). Recent driving models retain video prediction during training but predict trajectories directly at inference time, avoiding the computational cost of future-video generation (Zhao et al., 2026). Reinforcement learning can refine planner trained on demonstrations to explore alternative trajectories and learn from driving rewards (Zhou et al., 2025). However, driving logs contain future videos only for recorded trajectories. For example, when candidate turns while the recorded trajectory continues straight, the logged video does not show the visual consequences. Reusing such videos creates incorrect trajectory-video pairs, while omitting video training leaves these candidates without visual supervision. This creates supervision gap during post-training: current-policy trajectories lack matched future-video targets (Figure 1).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 1: From logged futures to candidate-matched supervision. (1) WAM pretraining uses the ground-truth (GT) trajectory and its logged future video. (2) Trajectory GRPO explores candidate trajectories using driving rewards, without matched video supervision. (3) World Engine renders reconstructed scenes along selected candidate paths, providing matched supervision independent of the models predictions. To address this gap, we introduce SIMVTA, simulation-grounded framework for video-trajectory alignment. WAMs own video predictions provide no external reference for checking whether they follow candidate trajectory. We use the 3DGS-based simulator in World Engine (Li et al., 2026c) to render reconstructed real-world scenes from camera poses along executed candidate paths (Figure 1). These renderings provide prediction-independent targets that match the scene geometry and motion of each selected trajectory, establishing video-trajectory alignment. We jointly train video prediction with flow matching and trajectory planning with GRPO, allowing the video loss to update shared representations. The former teaches the model to predict the visual consequences of candidate trajectories; the latter compares driving rewards among candidates and favors higher-reward trajectories. Rendering videos for every sampled trajectory is costly. We first select high-reward candidates for rendering, then prioritize video supervision for higher-error futures among the rendered candidates. This separates trajectory exploration from video-supervision target selection. Our ablations examine shared representation updates, target selection, trajectory-video correspondence, and online versus offline rendering. At inference, the planner predicts trajectories directly, without simulator calls or future-video generation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce SIMVTA, post-training framework that combines trajectory GRPO with simulatorbased video supervision. It connects policy sampling, trajectory execution, rendering, and joint updates to learn the visual consequences of actions beyond those recorded in driving logs. We introduce video-target selection strategy based on trajectory reward and video prediction error. It prioritizes higher-error futures of high-reward trajectories for video supervision without restricting trajectory exploration. Applying SIMVTA to WAM initialization improves NAVSIM v1 PDMS by 5.1 points, from 86.2 to 91.3, and achieves 88.2 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and an average HD-Score of 38.8 on HUGSIM.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: World Action Models. World models predict future observations or latent states to support driving simulation and planning (Wang et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2025c; Wang et al., 2026b;c; Jia et al., 2026a; Lu et al., 2026). Video-based approaches jointly model future frames and trajectories (Zhang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2026b; Shi et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 2: Simulation-grounded videotrajectory alignment. (a) Training overview. (b) Trajectory learning combines GRPO with behavior-cloning (BC) regularizer. (c) Video supervision selects high-reward, higher-error futures. (d) World Engine renders matched futures along executed paths. Video prediction can also be retained during training and omitted at inference, as explored in robotics by Fast-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026) and in driving by SimWAM (Zhao et al., 2026). SIMVTA focuses on trajectory-matched video supervision during driving WAM post-training. Simulation for Driving. Driving simulators support policy training and evaluation through controlled rollouts (Dosovitskiy et al., 2017; Li et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024; Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025a; Tian et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c; He et al., 2026). 3DGS (Kerbl et al., 2023) renders reconstructed scenes from specified camera poses, providing visual observations for closed-loop simulation (Zhou et al., 2024; NVIDIA et al., 2025a). World Engine (Li et al., 2026c) renders these observations along simulated ego motion for policy post-training. CausalDrive (Yan et al., 2026) instead uses learned renderer. SIMVTA uses World Engine to render video targets along selected candidate trajectories. Post-Training for Driving. Driving policies can be refined after initial training through reinforcement learning or model adaptation (Wang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2025b; Tang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026d; Zhou et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2026a). GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) has been applied to both diffusion and autoregressive planners (Li et al., 2026d; Tang et al., 2026). PlannerRFT (Li et al., 2026a) uses closed-loop reinforcement fine-tuning with adaptive exploration to improve diffusion planners. Our trajectory optimization uses the stochastic differential equation (SDE) sampling formulation from Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025). ReSim (Yang et al., 2025a) trains video simulator on simulated non-expert trajectories to improve action controllability. SIMVTA jointly updates shared representations through video prediction and trajectory GRPO.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: SIMVTAs post-training framework is illustrated in Figure 2 and comprises trajectory sampling, video rendering, and video supervision. We sample candidate trajectories from the current policy and execute them to obtain paths and driving rewards. World Engine (Li et al., 2026c) renders videos along selected paths during training. We select video targets based on trajectory reward and video prediction error, then update the model with trajectory GRPO and video supervision. The next sampling round uses the updated policy.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Implementation Details. We initialize SIMVTA from an Epona checkpoint adapted to NAVSIM as described in Appendix A, and perform post-training on NavTrain samples with available World Engine scene reconstructions. We use the 3DGS-based simulator in World Engine (Li et al., 2026c) to render matched future videos. In SIMVTA (Exp2), the video flow-matching loss uses Q2 targets and updates both the video network (VideoDiT) and the shared encoder. All ablations retain trajectory GRPO and the BC regularizer, with trajectory GRPO updating the shared encoder throughout. The mixed high/low-reward variants, Exp4 and Exp6, additionally apply the safety-specific advantage treatment described in Appendix D. Benchmarks and Metrics. We evaluate SIMVTA on the NavTest splits of NAVSIM v1 and v2 (Dauner et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2025), using PDMS and EPDMS, respectively, to assess safety, progress, and comfort. On HUGSIM (Zhou et al., 2024), we report route completion (RC) and HDScore, which combines RC with safety and comfort. Training uses the reward in Eq. 6; Benchmark scores follow their respective evaluation protocols. We report results averaged over three independent runs with different random seeds. sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 4: Qualitative planning comparison. Left: planned trajectories of SIMVTA (A, blue) and Epona (B, orange). Right: World Engine renderings along the corresponding paths at 14 s. Red boxes highlight Eponas collision and road-departure regions. 4.2 MAIN RESULTS NAVSIM. Starting from the NAVSIM-adapted Epona initialization at 86.2 PDMS, SIMVTA reaches 91.3 (+5.1) on NAVSIM v1 (Figure 3a; Table 1). Ego progress rises from 80.3 to 86.7, time-tocollision compliance from 93.9 to 97.0, and drivable-area compliance from 95.0 to 97.2. On NAVSIM v2, SIMVTA improves EPDMS from 85.0 to 88.2 (+3.2), and achieves 90.8 ego progress and 98.5 for both drivable-area and time-to-collision compliance  (Table 2)  . SIMVTA also improves planning in scenes where the Epona initialization fails (Figure 4). In these examples, Eponas trajectories lead to collision or leave the drivable area, whereas SIMVTA avoids the collision and stays within the drivable area. HUGSIM. We further evaluate the final planner in closed-loop driving on the same 345 prechallenge HUGSIM scenarios, using the same corrected evaluator and controller as Kirby et al. (2026). SIMVTA achieves the highest average RC (51.5) and HD-Score (38.8) among the compared methods, exceeding the reported DrivoR results by 1.7 and 3.1 points, respectively  (Table 3)  . It also leads on both metrics in hard scenarios, reaching 38.3 RC and 23.3 HD-Score. Video-Trajectory Alignment. Beyond the planning gains, we compare SIMVTA with Epona to examine whether post-training improves the consistency of predicted videos with the scene along trajectory (Figure 6). Epona generates an additional vehicle on the right (highlighted by red boxes) that is absent from both the birds-eye view (BEV) and the corresponding World Engine renderings. SIMVTA avoids this inconsistency in the illustrated scene. Video Quality. We evaluate both World Engine renderings and autoregressive model predictions against real videos on NAVSIM v1  (Table 4)  . Lower Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) indicate better video quality. Along logged GT trajectories, World Engine achieves an FID of 7.6 and an FVD of 21.8. Compared with trajectory GRPO alone (Exp0), SIMVTA reduces FID from 20.4 to 13.1 and FVD from 105.4 to 46.3, improving video prediction quality. Table 4: Video quality. Source 3DGS renderings World Engine WAM predictions Trajectory GRPO only (Exp0) SimVTA (Exp2) FID FVD 7.6 21.8 20.4 13.1 105.4 46.

Right: corresponding future frames rendered by the simulator. Colors match the paths and image rows. 4.3 ABLATION STUDIES Updating the Shared Representations. Video supervision improves planning when its gradients reach the shared encoder. Restricting video gradients to VideoDiT (Exp1) yields 89.1 PDMS, matching trajectory GRPO alone (Exp0; Figure 3a). Allowing video gradients to also update the shared encoder (Exp2) raises PDMS to 91.3 (+2.2)  (Table 5)  . Selecting Informative Futures. We compare video supervision across four candidate groups: Q1 (high reward, low error), Q2 (high reward, high error), Q3 (low reward, low error), and Q4 (low reward, high error). Highand low-reward candidates come from the top and bottom of the trajectory reward ranking, respectively. Within each scene, errors below the mean over valid rendered candidates are low; those at or above it are high. Q2 supervision yields the highest PDMS among the four settings. Exp2 uses Q2 supervision and achieves 91.3 PDMS. Exp5 uses the same high-reward rendering pool but expands video supervision to Q1+Q2, yielding 91.0 PDMS. Under the same high-reward rendering pool, focusing supervision on the higher-error Q2 subset performs better than supervising Q1+Q2. Exp4 and Exp6 use mixed high/low-reward pools with Q2+Q3 and Q1Q4 supervision, respectively, both achieving 90.9 PDMS  (Table 6)  . These two variants also apply the safety-specific advantage treatment described in Appendix D. Table 5: Ablation on shared encoder updates. In contrast, Exp2 first selects the higher-error Q2 subset according to ETF and then optimizes the selected targets with the flow-matching loss, reaching 91.3 PDMS  (Table 7)  . Both variants allow video gradients to update the shared encoder. This comparison tests whether selecting informative video targets before supervision is more effective than directly applying video GRPO to all valid rendered candidates. Comparing Online and Offline Rendering. We compare online rendering with fixed offline cache  (Table 8)  . Exp9 follows the same settings as Exp2, except that trajectories are sampled offline from the initial policy and their rendered videos are cached and reused throughout post-training. Exp2 instead refreshes video targets for current-policy trajectories. Exp9 achieves 90.4 PDMS, compared with 89.1 for trajectory-only Exp0 and 91.3 for Exp2, showing 0.9-point advantage for refreshing video targets from the current policy over using fixed initial-policy cache. Preserving Trajectory-Video Correspondence. To test whether the benefit depends on correct trajectory-video pairing rather than video supervision alone, Exp3 shuffles rendered targets across trajectory conditions within the same scene after selection. Breaking this alignment reduces PDMS from 91.3 (Exp2) to 83.1 (Exp3; Table 9), demonstrating the importance of preserving trajectoryvideo correspondence. Figure 5 shows the matched setting, where each target video is rendered along its corresponding path. Increasing the Rendering Budget. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented SIMVTA, simulation-grounded post-training framework that combines trajectory GRPO with video supervision. Rendering futures along current-policy trajectories provides visual targets beyond logged action-future pairs and jointly trains shared representations through video prediction and trajectory optimization. The full framework improves NAVSIM v1 PDMS from 86.2 to 91.3 (+5.1) and achieves 88.2 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 38.8 average HD-Score on HUGSIM. Ablations show that updating shared representations with video supervision improves planning, while prioritizing higher-error futures among high-reward trajectories further improves performance. Limitations and directions for future work are discussed in Appendix G.

sections.title: A TRAINING PROCEDURE
sections.content: Before applying SIMVTA, we fine-tune the nuPlan-pretrained Epona checkpoint on NAVSIM following the official adaptation recipe to adapt it from 10 Hz to 2 Hz. The adapted checkpoint initializes both Exp0 and Exp2. We evaluate it using the same NAVSIM v1 protocol as the posttrained models and obtain 86.2 PDMS, matching the overall score reported for Epona. Unless stated otherwise, the implementation details below describe Exp2. Training Loop. 1. Encode observation histories and sample trajectories, retaining their normalized denoising states. 2. Execute each candidate with PDM, compute its training reward, and normalize rewards within each observation group. 3. Check execution validity, pose support, and safety. Rank eligible candidates by reward and select the rendering pool. 4. Render the selected paths and encode their future frames, retaining the candidate-to-video correspondence. 5. Compute detached teacher-forced errors and classify the valid rendered candidates into quadrants. 6. Select the video-training subset and future frame for this update. Generate the detached BC teacher chain from the current shared representation. 7. Combine the trajectory loss, selected video loss, and BC regularizer. Update the trainable parameters and repeat with the updated policy. Architecture and Temporal Settings. Eponas spatiotemporal Transformer is the shared encoder, paired with TrajDiT and VideoDiT. Four observed frames condition eight trajectory waypoints spanning four seconds. PDM evaluates the path at 10 Hz; video pose conditions are sampled at 2 Hz. Exp2 computes teacher-forced prediction errors over future frames within the planning window and trains one sampled future frame per update. Trajectory Reward. Each candidate is scored together with the cached PDM reference trajectory. The training reward is Ri = NCi DACi 10 EPi + 5 TTCi + 2 Comforti 17 . (6) Following ReCogDrive (Li et al., 2026d), we use weights of 10, 5, and 2 for EP, TTC, and Comfort, respectively, with the higher EP weight encouraging efficient driving. The component scores lie in [0, 1]. Progress follows the PDM scorers normalization over the candidate and reference trajectories. Driving-direction compliance is used for candidate screening but has zero weight in this reward. Exp2 excludes video prediction error from trajectory rewards. Candidate Validity and Safety. An eligible video candidate must execute successfully and have finite pose changes within VideoDiTs support at every 2 Hz step: 0 16 m, 1.5 m, and yaw 32. Its maximum reverse speed must not exceed 103 m/s. For Exp2, the NC, DAC, TTC, and DDC scores must each be at least 0.999. We rank eligible candidates by Ri, break ties by sampling index, and select the first K. If fewer than qualify, only those candidates are rendered. Failed renders are excluded from video supervision. scene skips video supervision if all candidates fail the safety checks or its maximum reward is at most 106. These filters do not remove candidates from the Exp2 trajectory loss.

Exp0 uses trajectory GRPO and BC without video supervision. In Exp1, video gradients update only VideoDiT; trajectory and BC gradients still update the shared encoder. Exp2 also allows video gradients to update shared parameters. Both use Q2 targets. Exp3 shuffles rendered targets across trajectory conditions within scene after selection. Scenes without valid target permutation contribute no shuffled video supervision. Exp4 selects the two highestand two lowest-reward candidates from the executionand pose-valid pool. If this pool contains < 4 candidates, the high and low subsets contain n/2 and n/2 candidates, respectively. The subsets are disjoint, with reward ties broken by sampling index. Exp4 applies the four safety checks before training on Q2 and Q3. Exp5 renders four safe high-reward candidates and trains on all valid Q1 and Q2 candidates. Exp6 uses the same high/low pool as Exp4 but trains on all valid rendered candidates, including individually unsafe candidates. In Exp4 and Exp6, an unsafe candidates positive trajectory advantage is additionally truncated to zero: Ai min(Ai, 0). Exp2 does not apply this projection. Exp7 increases the rendering budget from four to eight while retaining Exp2s Q2 selection and video-training rule. Both settings train on all valid Q2 candidates. Table 12 distinguishes the rendered pool from the subset used for video training. Fixed Offline Cache (Exp9). Exp9 follows the same experimental settings as Exp2, except that trajectories are sampled offline from the initial model and their rendered videos are stored in fixed cache. The cached trajectory-video pairs are reused throughout post-training. All other settings, including candidate selection, rendering budget, training objectives, and optimization hyperparameters, are identical to Exp2. The reward is the negative framewise latent MSE, aggregated with normalized temporal weights proportional to 0.85r1. It does not include the motion-weighted temporal-change term in Eq. 9. Different trajectory conditions within the same scene form the video comparison group. The video policy objective uses group-normalized advantages and clipped ratio computed from dimension-normalized Gaussian log densities, with clipping parameter 0.2. One future frame is replayed for optimization per update, cycling through the video horizon. Groups with fewer than two valid candidates or reward standard deviation below 106 contribute no video policy update. Video GRPO replaces video flow matching and updates VideoDiT and shared parameters; its reward does not enter trajectory advantages. Rendering and Optimization Budgets. specifies the number of candidates budgeted for rendering; Table 12 separately lists those used for video training. Error-based selection follows rendering and scoring, so these costs apply to every rendered candidate. Total training cost also includes trajectory sampling, PDM evaluation, video optimization, and optimizer updates. Comparisons at equal match rendering caps, while video optimization costs depend on the training subset and objective. Exp9 renders its cache once; Exp2 renders candidates at each sampling round. Interpreting the Ablations. Table 12 summarizes the supervision configurations underlying the main-text ablations. For Exp3, scenes without valid within-scene target permutation contribute no shuffled video supervision. Exp2 and Exp5 compare Q2 versus Q1+Q2 supervision from the same rendering pool, although the number of video-training candidates differs. Exp4 and Exp6 additionally modify the safety-specific treatment of trajectory advantages and are therefore interpreted as broader configuration comparisons. Results across Random Seeds. Table 14 reports NAVSIM v1 PDMS for Exp0, Exp2, Exp5, and Exp7 across three random seeds. Exp2 outperforms the other three variants on every seed.

sections.title: E VIDEO SUPERVISION AND EVALUATION
sections.content: The teacher-forced error quantifies model prediction consistency against rendered simulation targets given preceding reference frames. We separately evaluate renderer fidelity, autoregressive video generation quality, and action-conditioning accuracy. Renderer Fidelity. We compare front-view World Engine renderings along logged GT trajectories with real observations on NAVSIM v1 NavTest. Each clip contains eight future frames over four seconds at 2 Hz. FID is computed on frames and FVD on clips using the same preprocessing and feature extractors for the two domains. These measurements quantify rendering fidelity at logged viewpoints; novel-view coverage is discussed in Appendix G. Model Video Quality. sections.title: G LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Reconstruction Quality and Coverage. Occlusions and limited pose coverage can degrade renderings away from logged paths, while renderer metrics assess only logged viewpoints. Even with safety and pose-support checks, rendering artifacts can still appear. high prediction error can stem from either model limitations or poor-quality simulation targets. Quality-aware filtering and evaluation at alternative poses remain necessary.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 7: Reported planning results across benchmarks. (a) NAVSIM v1 PDMS and v2 EPDMS, with NAVSIM v2 component-score differences (SIMVTA minus the NAVSIM-adapted Epona initialization). (b) HUGSIM RC and HD-Score using benchmark aggregation. (c) RC and (d) HD-Score for DrivoR and SIMVTA by scenario difficulty. Values correspond to Tables 1, 2, and 3. Distribution Shifts. Current-policy trajectories broaden action coverage, but observation histories remain log-based and rendered targets can differ from real images. Reconstruction coverage and candidate filtering further limit supervision. Teacher-forced selection cannot capture autoregressive error accumulation. We leave robustness evaluation under shifted observation histories and reactive traffic (Jia et al., 2024; 2026b) for future work. Architecture and Training Cost. We validate our framework based on the Epona backbone. Generalization to alternative WAM architectures is left for future work. Online rendering, error scoring, and video optimization increase training cost, while inference uses direct trajectory prediction.
